Use ``nx.is_tree(G)`` to check.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    G : NetworkX graph\n        A tree graph (undirected, acyclic graph).\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    center : list\n        A list of nodes forming the center of the tree. Classes provide node, edge and degree \"views\" of a graph.\n\nViews for nodes, edges and degree are provided for all base graph classes.\nA view means a read-only object that is quick to create, automatically\nupdated when the graph changes, and provides basic access like `n in V`,\n`for n in V`, `V[n]` and sometimes set operations.\n\nThe views are read-only iterable containers that are updated as the\ngraph is updated. As with dicts, the graph should not be updated\nwhile iterating through the view. Views can be iterated multiple times.\n\nEdge and Node views also allow data attribute lookup.\nThe resulting attribute dict is writable as `G.edges[3, 4]['color']='red'`\nDegree views allow lookup of degree values for single nodes.\nWeighted degree is supported with the `weight` argument.\n\nNodeView\n========\n\n    `V = G.nodes` (or `V = G.nodes()`) allows `len(V)`, `n in V`, set\n    operations e.g. \"G.nodes & H.nodes\", and `dd = G.nodes[n]`, where\n    `dd` is the node data dict. Iteration is over the nodes by default.\n\nNodeDataView\n============\n\n    To iterate over (node, data) pairs, use arguments to `G.nodes()`\n    to create a DataView e.g. `DV = G.nodes(data='color', default='red')`.\n    The DataView iterates as `for n, color in DV` and allows\n    `(n, 'red') in DV`. Using `DV = G.nodes(data=True)`, the DataViews\n    use the full datadict in writeable form also allowing contain testing as\n    `(n, {'color': 'red'}) in VD`. DataViews allow set operations when\n    data attributes are hashable.\n\nDegreeView\n==========\n\n    `V = G.degree` allows iteration over (node, degree) pairs as well\n    as lookup: `deg=V[n]`. There are many flavors of DegreeView\n    for In/Out/Directed/Multi. For Directed Graphs, `G.degree`\n    counts both in and out going edges. `G.out_degree` and\n    `G.in_degree` count only specific directions.\n    Weighted degree using edge data attributes is provide via\n    `V = G.degree(weight='attr_name')` where any string with the\n    attribute name can be used. `weight=None` is the default.\n    No set operations are implemented for degrees, use NodeView.\n\n    The argument `nbunch` restricts iteration to nodes in nbunch.\n    The DegreeView can still lookup any node even if nbunch is specified.\n\nEdgeView\n========\n\n    `V = G.edges` or `V = G.edges()` allows iteration over edges as well as\n    `e in V`, set operations and edge data lookup `dd = G.edges[2, 3]`.\n    Iteration is over 2-tuples `(u, v)` for Graph/DiGraph. For multigraphs\n    edges 3-tuples `(u, v, key)` are the default but 2-tuples can be obtained\n    via `V = G.edges(keys=False)`.\n\n    Set operations for directed graphs treat the edges as a set of 2-tuples.\n    For undirected graphs, 2-tuples are not a unique representation of edges.\n    So long as the set being compared to contains unique representations\n    of its edges, the set operations will act as expected. If the other\n    set contains both `(0, 1)` and `(1, 0)` however, the result of set\n    operations may contain both representations of the same edge.\n\nEdgeDataView\n============\n\n    Edge data can be reported using an EdgeDataView typically created\n    by calling an EdgeView: `DV = G.edges(data='weight', default=1)`.\n    The EdgeDataView allows iteration over edge tuples, membership checking\n    but no set operations.\n\n    Iteration depends on `data` and `default` and for multigraph `keys`\n    If `data is False` (the default) then iterate over 2-tuples `(u, v)`.\n    If `data is True` iterate over 3-tuples `(u, v, datadict)`.\n    Otherwise iterate over `(u, v, datadict.get(data, default))`.\n    For Multigraphs, if `keys is True`, replace `u, v` with `u, v, key`\n    to create 3-tuples and 4-tuples.\n\n    The argument `nbunch` restricts edges to those incident to nodes in nbunch.\n\"\"\"\n\nfrom abc import ABC\nfrom collections.abc import Mapping, Set\n\nimport networkx as nx\n\n__all__ = [\n    \"NodeView\",\n    \"NodeDataView\",\n    \"EdgeView\",\n    \"OutEdgeView\",\n    \"InEdgeView\",\n    \"EdgeDataView\",\n    \"OutEdgeDataView\",\n    \"InEdgeDataView\",\n    \"MultiEdgeView\",\n    \"OutMultiEdgeView\",\n    \"InMultiEdgeView\",\n    \"MultiEdgeDataView\",\n    \"OutMultiEdgeDataView\",\n    \"InMultiEdgeDataView\",\n    \"DegreeView\",\n    \"DiDegreeView\",\n    \"InDegreeView\",\n    \"OutDegreeView\",\n    \"MultiDegreeView\",\n    \"DiMultiDegreeView\",\n    \"InMultiDegreeView\",\n    \"OutMultiDegreeView\",\n]\n\n\n# NodeViews\nclass NodeView(Mapping, Set):\n    \"\"\"A NodeView class to act as G.nodes for a NetworkX Graph\n\n    Set operations act on the nodes without considering data.\n    Iteration is over nodes. (Lederberg-Coxeter-Fruchte) notation[1]_ is a compressed\n    notation used in the generation of various cubic Hamiltonian\n    graphs of high symmetry. See, for example, `dodecahedral_graph`,\n    `desargues_graph`, `heawood_graph` and `pappus_graph`.\n\n    Nodes are drawn from ``range(n)``. Each node ``n_i`` is connected with\n    node ``n_i + shift % n`` where ``shift`` is given by cycling through\n    the input `shift_list` `repeat` s times.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    n : int\n       The starting graph is the `n`-cycle with nodes ``0, ..., n-1``.\n       The null graph is returned if `n` < 1.\n\n    shift_list : list\n       A list of integer shifts mod `n`, ``[s1, s2, .., sk]``\n\n    repeats : int\n       Integer specifying the number of times that shifts in `shift_list`\n       are successively applied to each current node in the n-cycle\n       to generate an edge between ``n_current`` and ``n_current + shift mod n``.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    G : Graph\n       A graph instance created from the specified LCF notation.\n\n    Examples\n    --------\n    The utility graph $K_{3,3}$\n\n    >>> G = nx.LCF_graph(6, [3, -3], 3)\n    >>> G.edges()\n    EdgeView([(0, 1), (0, 5), (0, 3), (1, 2), (1, 4), (2, 3), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 5)])\n\n    The Heawood graph:\n\n    >>> G = nx.LCF_graph(14, [5, -5], 7)\n    >>> nx.is_isomorphic(G, nx.heawood_graph())\n    True\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. Join vertex $j$ of $P_h$ to vertex $h·i+j$ of $Q_i$ [3]_.\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. [1] https://blogs.ams.org/visualinsight/2016/02/01/hoffman-singleton-graph/\n    .. [2] https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Hoffman-SingletonGraph.html\n    .. [3] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoffman%E2%80%93Singleton_graph\n\n    \"\"\"\n    G = nx.Graph()\n    for i in range(5):\n        for j in range(5):\n            G.add_edge((\"pentagon\", i, j), (\"pentagon\", i, (j - 1) % 5))\n            G.add_edge((\"pentagon\", i, j), (\"pentagon\", i, (j + 1) % 5))\n            G.add_edge((\"pentagram\", i, j), (\"pentagram\", i, (j - 2) % 5))\n            G.add_edge((\"pentagram\", i, j), (\"pentagram\", i, (j + 2) % 5))\n            for k in range(5):\n                G.add_edge((\"pentagon\", i, j), (\"pentagram\", k, (i * k + j) % 5))\n    G = nx.convert_node_labels_to_integers(G)\n    G.name = \"Hoffman-Singleton Graph\"\n    return G\n\n\n@_raise_on_directed\n@nx._dispatchable(graphs=None, returns_graph=True)\ndef house_graph(create_using=None):\n    \"\"\"\n    Returns the House graph (square with triangle on top)\n\n    The house graph is a simple undirected graph with\n    5 nodes and 6 edges [1]_.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    create_using : NetworkX graph constructor, optional (default=nx.Graph)\n       Graph type to create. If graph instance, then cleared before populated.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    G : networkx Graph\n        Generalized Petersen Graph n k\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. [1] https://mathworld.wolfram.com/GeneralizedPetersenGraph.html\n    .. [2] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_Petersen_graph\n    \"\"\"\n    if n <= 2:\n        raise NetworkXError(f\"n >= 3 required. Got {n=}\")\n    if k < 1 or k > n / 2:\n        raise NetworkXError(f\" Got {n=} {k=}. Need 1 <= k <= n/2\")\n\n    G = nx.cycle_graph(range(n), create_using=create_using)  # u-nodes\n    if G.is_directed():\n        raise NetworkXError(\"Directed Graph not supported in create_using\")\n    for i in range(n):\n        G.add_edge(i, n + i)  # add v-nodes and u to v edges\n        G.add_edge(n + i, n + (i + k) % n)  # edge from v_i to v_(i+k)%n\n\n    G.name = f\"Generalized Petersen Graph GP({n}, {k})\"\n    return G\n\n\n@nx._dispatchable(graphs=None, returns_graph=True)\ndef sedgewick_maze_graph(create_using=None):\n    \"\"\"\n    Return a small maze with a cycle.\n\n    This is the maze used in Sedgewick, 3rd Edition, Part 5, Graph\n    Algorithms, Chapter 18, e.g. Figure 18.2 and following [1]_.\n    Nodes are numbered 0,..,7\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    create_using : NetworkX graph constructor, optional (default=nx.Graph)\n       Graph type to create. LCF notation.\n\n    LCF (Lederberg-Coxeter-Fruchte) notation[1]_ is a compressed\n    notation used in the generation of various cubic Hamiltonian\n    graphs of high symmetry. See, for example, `dodecahedral_graph`,\n    `desargues_graph`, `heawood_graph` and `pappus_graph`.\n\n    Nodes are drawn from ``range(n)``. Each node ``n_i`` is connected with\n    node ``n_i + shift % n`` where ``shift`` is given by cycling through\n    the input `shift_list` `repeat` s times.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    n : int\n       The starting graph is the `n`-cycle with nodes ``0, ..., n-1``.\n       The null graph is returned if `n` < 1.\n\n    shift_list : list\n       A list of integer shifts mod `n`, ``[s1, s2, .., sk]``\n\n    repeats : int\n       Integer specifying the number of times that shifts in `shift_list`\n       are successively applied to each current node in the n-cycle\n       to generate an edge between ``n_current`` and ``n_current + shift mod n``.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    G : Graph\n       A graph instance created from the specified LCF notation.\n\n    Examples\n    --------\n    The utility graph $K_{3,3}$\n\n    >>> G = nx.LCF_graph(6, [3, -3], 3)\n    >>> G.edges()\n    EdgeView([(0, 1), (0, 5), (0, 3), (1, 2), (1, 4), (2, 3), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 5)])\n\n    The Heawood graph:\n\n    >>> G = nx.LCF_graph(14, [5, -5], 7)\n    >>> nx.is_isomorphic(G, nx.heawood_graph())\n    True\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. The copies ``(v, 0), (v, 1), ..., (v, k - 1)`` of a node `v`\n    form the *fibre* of `v`. Every edge ``(u, v)`` of `G` is realised in the\n    lift as a perfect matching between the fibre of `u` and the fibre of `v`:\n    a permutation $\\pi$ of ``range(k)`` is chosen uniformly at random and the\n    edges ``((u, i), (v, pi[i]))`` are added for every ``i`` in ``range(k)``.\n    Each edge of `G` receives its own independent permutation [1]_ [2]_.\n\n    The map ``(v, i) -> v`` is a covering map from the lift onto `G`, so every\n    copy ``(v, i)`` has the same degree as `v` (when `G` has no self-loops)\n    and the lift of a `d`-regular graph is again `d`-regular. Random lifts\n    are a standard tool to build (nearly Ramanujan) expander graphs [2]_.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    G : NetworkX graph\n        The base graph. Directed graphs and multigraphs are supported: an arc\n        ``(u, v)`` lifts to arcs from the fibre of `u` to the fibre of `v`,\n        and every parallel edge is lifted independently.\n\n    k : int\n        The number of copies of each node (the order of the lift). Must be a\n        positive integer.\n\n    seed : integer, random_state, or None (default)\n        Indicator of random number generation state.\n        See :ref:`Randomness<randomness>`.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    H : NetworkX graph\n        A graph of the same type as `G` whose nodes are the pairs ``(v, i)``\n        for each node `v` of `G` and each ``i`` in ``range(k)``. Graph, node\n        and edge attributes of `G` are copied onto the lift.\n\n    Raises\n    ------\n    NetworkXError\n        If `k` is not a positive integer.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    A self-loop at `v` lifts to the edges ``((v, i), (v, pi[i]))``, i.e. to\n    the cycle structure of the random permutation on the fibre of `v`. For\n    graph types that do not allow parallel edges, coinciding lifted edges are\n    merged.\n\n    Examples\n    --------\n    >>> G = nx.complete_graph(4)\n    >>> H = nx.random_k_lift(G, 3, seed=42)\n    >>> H.number_of_nodes(), H.number_of_edges()\n    (12, 18)\n    >>> all(d == 3 for _, d in H.degree)\n    True\n    >>> sorted(v for v in H if v[0] == 0)\n    [(0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2)]\n\n    Every edge of `G` becomes a perfect matching between two fibres:\n\n    >>> sorted(i for (a, i), (b, j) in H.edges if {a, b} == {0, 1})\n    [0, 1, 2]\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. [1] Alon Amit and Nathan Linial,\n       \"Random graph coverings I: General theory and graph connectivity\",\n       *Combinatorica* 22 (2002): 1--18.\n    .. [2] Yonatan Bilu and Nathan Linial,\n       \"Lifts, discrepancy and nearly optimal spectral gap\",\n       *Combinatorica* 26 (2006): 495--519.\n    \"\"\"\n    try:\n        order = operator.index(k)\n    except TypeError as err:\n        raise nx.NetworkXError(f\"k must be a positive integer, got {k!r}\") from err\n    if order < 1:\n        raise nx.NetworkXError(f\"k must be a positive integer, got {k!r}\")\n\n    H = G.__class__()\n    H.graph.update(G.graph)\n    H.add_nodes_from(((v, i), dd) for v, dd in G._node.items() for i in range(order))\n    if G.is_multigraph():\n        edges = ((u, v, dd) for u, v, _, dd in G.edges(keys=True, data=True))\n    else:\n        edges = G.edges(data=True)\n    for u, v, dd in edges:\n        perm = list(range(order))\n        seed.shuffle(perm)\n        H.add_edges_from(((u, i), (v, j), dd) for i, j in enumerate(perm))\n    return H\nEOF\npython - <<'EOF'\nimport re\np = \"networkx/generators/random_graphs.py\"\ns = open(p).read()\ns = s.replace('    \"random_kernel_graph\",\\n]', '    \"random_kernel_graph\",\\n    \"random_k_lift\",\\n]', 1)\ns = s.replace(\"import itertools\\nimport math\\n\", \"import itertools\\nimport math\\nimport operator\\n\", 1)\nopen(p, \"w\").write(s)\nEOF\nsed -n 1,40p networkx/generators/random_graphs.py | head -40","description":"Add random_k_lift generator"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":3670,"cache_read_input_tokens":330597,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":3670,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":3,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"b95cb73d-2f43-4955-8eef-66dab11340b3","uuid":"215c0342-0689-4df4-b31a-2e706605a223","timestamp":"2026-11-17T08:24:26.349Z","request_id":"req_011Ch8BLqxbMYsrYuJUAH98y"}

With $A$ the weighted adjacency matrix,\n    let\n\n    .. math::\n\n        A_s = \\frac{1}{2}(A + A^T), \\qquad\n        \\Theta^{(q)} = 2 \\pi q (A - A^T), \\qquad\n        D_s = \\operatorname{diag}(A_s \\mathbf{1}).\n\n    The magnetic Laplacian is\n\n    .. math::\n\n        L^{(q)} = D_s - A_s \\odot \\exp(i \\Theta^{(q)}),\n\n    where $\\odot$ is the entry-wise product and the exponential is taken\n    entry-wise. The normalized magnetic Laplacian is\n    $D_s^{-1/2} L^{(q)} D_s^{-1/2}$, that is\n    $I - D_s^{-1/2} \\left(A_s \\odot \\exp(i \\Theta^{(q)})\\right) D_s^{-1/2}$\n    for nodes with nonzero degree.\n\n    An edge ``(u, v)`` without a reciprocal edge ``(v, u)`` contributes the\n    phase $e^{2 \\pi i q w}$ to entry ``(u, v)`` and the conjugate phase to\n    entry ``(v, u)``, where $w$ is its weight. Reciprocal edges of equal\n    weight, and hence all edges of undirected graphs, carry no phase.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    G : graph\n       A NetworkX graph\n\n    nodelist : list, optional\n       The rows and columns are ordered according to the nodes in `nodelist`.\n       If `nodelist` is None, then the ordering is produced by ``G.nodes()``.\n\n    normalized : bool, optional (default=False)\n       If True, return the symmetrically normalized magnetic Laplacian\n       $D_s^{-1/2} L^{(q)} D_s^{-1/2}$.\n\n    q : float, optional (default=0.25)\n       The charge parameter that sets the size of the phase. With ``q=0`` the\n       magnetic Laplacian is the Laplacian of the symmetrized graph $A_s$.\n       Values in ``[0, 1/2]`` cover all distinct behaviours for unweighted\n       graphs and ``q=1/4`` maximally separates the two directions of an edge.\n\n    weight : string or None, optional (default='weight')\n       The edge data key used to compute each value in the matrix.\n       If None, then each edge has weight 1.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    L : SciPy sparse array\n      The (complex, Hermitian) magnetic Laplacian matrix of `G`.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    For MultiGraph/MultiDiGraph, the edges weights are summed.\n    Self-loops contribute to $A_s$ and $D_s$ without a phase, so (as for\n    :func:`laplacian_matrix`) they cancel on the diagonal of the\n    unnormalized matrix.\n\n    For undirected graphs the magnetic Laplacian equals the Laplacian\n    (:func:`laplacian_matrix`) and its normalized version equals\n    :func:`normalized_laplacian_matrix`, for every value of `q`.\n\n    The magnetic Laplacian is positive semidefinite, so its eigenvalues are\n    real and non-negative. See :func:`~networkx.linalg.spectrum.magnetic_spectrum`.\n\n    Examples\n    --------\n    >>> import numpy as np\n    >>> G = nx.DiGraph([(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0)])\n    >>> L = nx.magnetic_laplacian_matrix(G)\n    >>> L[0, 1], L[1, 0]\n    (np.complex128(-0.5j), np.complex128(0.5j))\n    >>> np.allclose(L.toarray(), L.toarray().conj().T)  # Hermitian\n    True\n\n    Undirected graphs carry no phase:\n\n    >>> H = nx.path_graph(4)\n    >>> np.allclose(nx.magnetic_laplacian_matrix(H).toarray(), nx.laplacian_matrix(H).toarray())\n    True\n\n    See Also\n    --------\n    laplacian_matrix\n    normalized_laplacian_matrix\n    magnetic_spectrum\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. Suykens,\n       \"Magnetic Eigenmaps for the Visualization of Directed Networks\",\n       Applied and Computational Harmonic Analysis, 44 (2018), pp. 189--199.\n    .. [2] X. Zhang, Y. He, N. Brugnone, M. Perlmutter and M. A^T generating the phase.\n    # Both are built from the same coordinates, so after summing duplicates\n    # their entries are stored in the same (canonical) order.\n    sym = sp.sparse.coo_array(\n        (np.concatenate((A.data, A.data)) / 2, (rows, cols)), shape=(n, n)\n    )\n    antisym = sp.sparse.coo_array(\n        (np.concatenate((A.data, -A.data)), (rows, cols)), shape=(n, n)\n    )\n    sym.sum_duplicates()\n    antisym.sum_duplicates()\n    phase = np.exp(2j * np.pi * q * antisym.data)\n    H = sp.sparse.coo_array((sym.data * phase, (sym.row, sym.col)), shape=(n, n))\n    diags = sym.sum(axis=1)\n    D = sp.sparse.dia_array((diags, 0), shape=(n, n))\n    L = (D - With $A$ the weighted adjacency matrix,\n    let\n\n    .. math::\n\n        A_s = \\frac{1}{2}(A + A^T), \\qquad\n        \\Theta^{(q)} = 2 \\pi q (A - A^T), \\qquad\n        D_s = \\operatorname{diag}(A_s \\mathbf{1}).\n\n    The magnetic Laplacian is\n\n    .. math::\n\n        L^{(q)} = D_s - A_s \\odot \\exp(i \\Theta^{(q)}),\n\n    where $\\odot$ is the entry-wise product and the exponential is taken\n    entry-wise. The normalized magnetic Laplacian is\n    $D_s^{-1/2} L^{(q)} D_s^{-1/2}$, that is\n    $I - D_s^{-1/2} \\left(A_s \\odot \\exp(i \\Theta^{(q)})\\right) D_s^{-1/2}$\n    for nodes with nonzero degree.\n\n    An edge ``(u, v)`` without a reciprocal edge ``(v, u)`` contributes the\n    phase $e^{2 \\pi i q w}$ to entry ``(u, v)`` and the conjugate phase to\n    entry ``(v, u)``, where $w$ is its weight. Reciprocal edges of equal\n    weight, and hence all edges of undirected graphs, carry no phase.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    G : graph\n       A NetworkX graph\n\n    nodelist : list, optional\n       The rows and columns are ordered according to the nodes in `nodelist`.\n       If `nodelist` is None, then the ordering is produced by ``G.nodes()``.\n\n    normalized : bool, optional (default=False)\n       If True, return the symmetrically normalized magnetic Laplacian\n       $D_s^{-1/2} L^{(q)} D_s^{-1/2}$.\n\n    q : float, optional (default=0.25)\n       The charge parameter that sets the size of the phase. With ``q=0`` the\n       magnetic Laplacian is the Laplacian of the symmetrized graph $A_s$.\n       Values in ``[0, 1/2]`` cover all distinct behaviours for unweighted\n       graphs and ``q=1/4`` maximally separates the two directions of an edge.\n\n    weight : string or None, optional (default='weight')\n       The edge data key used to compute each value in the matrix.\n       If None, then each edge has weight 1.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    L : SciPy sparse array\n      The (complex, Hermitian) magnetic Laplacian matrix of `G`.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    For MultiGraph/MultiDiGraph, the edges weights are summed.\n    Self-loops contribute to $A_s$ and $D_s$ without a phase, so (as for\n    :func:`laplacian_matrix`) they cancel on the diagonal of the\n    unnormalized matrix.\n\n    For undirected graphs the magnetic Laplacian equals the Laplacian\n    (:func:`laplacian_matrix`) and its normalized version equals\n    :func:`normalized_laplacian_matrix`, for every value of `q`.\n\n    The magnetic Laplacian is positive semidefinite, so its eigenvalues are\n    real and non-negative. See :func:`~networkx.linalg.spectrum.magnetic_spectrum`.\n\n    Examples\n    --------\n    >>> import numpy as np\n    >>> G = nx.DiGraph([(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0)])\n    >>> L = nx.magnetic_laplacian_matrix(G)\n    >>> print(np.round(L.toarray(), 6) + 0)\n    [[ 1.+0.j  -0.-0.5j -0.+0.5j]\n     [-0.+0.5j  1.+0.j  -0.-0.5j]\n     [-0.-0.5j -0.+0.5j  1.+0.j ]]\n    >>> np.allclose(L.toarray(), L.toarray().conj().T)  # Hermitian\n    True\n\n    Undirected graphs carry no phase:\n\n    >>> H = nx.path_graph(4)\n    >>> np.allclose(nx.magnetic_laplacian_matrix(H).toarray(), nx.laplacian_matrix(H).toarray())\n    True\n\n    See Also\n    --------\n    laplacian_matrix\n    normalized_laplacian_matrix\n    magnetic_spectrum\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. [1] M. Fanuel, C. M. Alaíz, Á. Fernández and J. A. K. Suykens,\n       \"Magnetic Eigenmaps for the Visualization of Directed Networks\",\n       Applied and Computational Harmonic Analysis, 44 (2018), pp. 189--199.\n    .. [2] X. Zhang, Y. He, N. Brugnone, M. Perlmutter and M. Hirn,\n       \"MagNet: A Neural Network for Directed Graphs\",\n       Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021).\n    \"\"\"\n    import numpy as np\n    import scipy as sp\n\n    if nodelist is None:\n        nodelist = list(G)\n    A = nx.to_scipy_sparse_array(\n        G, nodelist=nodelist, weight=weight, dtype=float, format=\"coo\"\n    )\n    n = A.shape[0]\n    # Entries of A and of its transpose, on the union of both sparsity patterns.\n    rows = np.concatenate((A.row, A.col))\n    cols = np.concatenate((A.col, A.row))\n    # A_s = (A + A^T) / 2 and the antisymmetric part A - A^T generating the phase.\n    # Both are built from the same coordinates, so after summing duplicates\n    # their entries are stored in the same (canonical) order.\n    sym = sp.sparse.coo_array(\n        (np.concatenate((A.data, A.data)) / 2, (rows, cols)), shape=(n, n)\n    )\n    antisym = sp.sparse.coo_array(\n        (np.concatenate((A.data, -A.data)), (rows, cols)), shape=(n, n)\n    )\n    sym.sum_duplicates()\n    antisym.sum_duplicates()\n    phase = np.exp(2j * np.pi * q * antisym.data)\n    H = sp.sparse.coo_array((sym.data * phase, (sym.row, sym.col)), shape=(n, n))\n    diags = sym.sum(axis=1)\n    D = sp.sparse.dia_array((diags, 0), shape=(n, n))\n    L = (D - H).tocsr()\n    if not normalized:\n        return L\n    with np.errstate(divide=\"ignore\"):\n        diags_sqrt = 1.0 / np.sqrt(diags)\n    diags_sqrt[np.isinf(diags_sqrt)] = 0\n    DH = sp.sparse.dia_array((diags_sqrt, 0), shape=(n, n)).tocsr()\n    return DH @ (L @ DH)\n\n\n###############################################################################\n# Code based on work from https://github.com/bjedwards\n\n\n@not_implemented_for(\"undirected\")\n@not_implemented_for(\"multigraph\")\n@nx._dispatchable(edge_attrs=\"weight\")\ndef directed_laplacian_matrix(\n    G, nodelist=None, weight=\"weight\", walk_type=None, alpha=0.95\n):\n    r\"\"\"Returns the directed Laplacian matrix of G.\n\n    The graph directed Laplacian is the matrix\n\n    .. math::\n\n        L = I - \\frac{1}{2} \\left (\\Phi^{1/2} P \\Phi^{-1/2} + \\Phi^{-1/2} P^T \\Phi^{1/2} \\right )\n\n    where `I` is the identity matrix, `P` is the transition matrix of the\n    graph, and `\\Phi` a matrix with the Perron vector of `P` in the diagonal and\n    zeros elsewhere [1]_.\n\n    Depending on the value of walk_type, `P` can be the transition matrix\n    induced by a random walk, a lazy random walk, or a random walk with\n    teleportation (PageRank).\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    G : DiGraph\n       A NetworkX graph\n\n    nodelist : list, optional\n       The rows and columns are ordered according to the nodes in nodelist.\n       If nodelist is None, then the ordering is produced by G.nodes().\n\n    weight : string or None, optional (default='weight')\n       The edge data key used to compute each value in the matrix.\n       If None, then each edge has weight 1.\n\n    walk_type : string or None, optional (default=None)\n       One of ``\"random\"``, ``\"lazy\"``, or ``\"pagerank\"``. If ``walk_type=None``\n       (the default), then a value is selected according to the properties of `G`:\n       - ``walk_type=\"random\"`` if `G` is strongly connected and aperiodic\n       - ``walk_type=\"lazy\"`` if `G` is strongly connected but not aperiodic\n       - ``walk_type=\"pagerank\"`` for all other cases.\n\n    alpha : real\n       (1 - alpha) is the teleportation probability used with pagerank\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    L : NumPy matrix\n      Normalized Laplacian of G.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    Only implemented for DiGraphs\n\n    The result is always a symmetric matrix.\n\n    This calculation uses the out-degree of the graph `G`. To use the\n    in-degree for calculations instead, use `G.reverse(copy=False)` and\n    take the transpose.\n\n    See Also\n    --------\n    laplacian_matrix\n    normalized_laplacian_matrix\n    directed_combinatorial_laplacian_matrix\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. [1] Fan Chung (2005).\n       Laplacians and the Cheeger inequality for directed graphs.\n       Annals of Combinatorics, 9(1), 2005\n    \"\"\"\n    import numpy as np\n    import scipy as sp\n\n    # NOTE: P has type ndarray if walk_type==\"pagerank\", else csr_array\n    P = _transition_matrix(\n        G, nodelist=nodelist, weight=weight, walk_type=walk_type, alpha=alpha\n    )\n\n    n, m = P.shape\n\n    evals, evecs = sp.sparse.linalg.eigs(P.T, k=1)\n    v = evecs.flatten().real\n    p = v / v.sum()\n    # p>=0 by Perron-Frobenius Thm. Use abs() to fix roundoff across zero gh-6865\n    sqrtp = np.sqrt(np.abs(p))\n    Q = (\n        sp.sparse.dia_array((sqrtp, 0), shape=(n, n)).tocsr()\n        @ P\n        @ sp.sparse.dia_array((1.0 / sqrtp, 0), shape=(n, n)).tocsr()\n    )\n    # NOTE: This could be sparsified for the non-pagerank cases\n    I = np.identity(len(G))\n\n    return I - (Q + Q.T) / 2.0\n\n\n@not_implemented_for(\"undirected\")\n@not_implemented_for(\"multigraph\")\n@nx._dispatchable(edge_attrs=\"weight\")\ndef directed_combinatorial_laplacian_matrix(\n    G, nodelist=None, weight=\"weight\", walk_type=None, alpha=0.95\n):\n    r\"\"\"Return the directed combinatorial Laplacian matrix of G.\n\n    The graph directed combinatorial Laplacian is the matrix\n\n    .. math::\n\n        L = \\Phi - \\frac{1}{2} \\left (\\Phi P + P^T \\Phi \\right)\n\n    where `P` is the transition matrix of the graph and `\\Phi` a matrix\n    with the Perron vector of `P` in the diagonal and zeros elsewhere [1]_.\n\n    Depending on the value of walk_type, `P` can be the transition matrix\n    induced by a random walk, a lazy random walk, or a random walk with\n    teleportation (PageRank).\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    G : DiGraph\n       A NetworkX graph\n\n    nodelist : list, optional\n       The rows and columns are ordered according to the nodes in nodelist.\n       If nodelist is None, then the ordering is produced by G.nodes().\n\n    weight : string or None, optional (default='weight')\n       The edge data key used to compute each value in the matrix.\n       If None, then each edge has weight 1.\n\n    walk_type : string or None, optional (default=None)\n        One of ``\"random\"``, ``\"lazy\"``, or ``\"pagerank\"``. If ``walk_type=None``\n        (the default), then a value is selected according to the properties of `G`:\n        - ``walk_type=\"random\"`` if `G` is strongly connected and aperiodic\n        - ``walk_type=\"lazy\"`` if `G` is strongly connected but not aperiodic\n        - ``walk_type=\"pagerank\"`` for all other cases.\n\n    alpha : real\n       (1 - alpha) is the teleportation probability used with pagerank\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    L : NumPy matrix\n      Combinatorial Laplacian of G.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    Only implemented for DiGraphs\n\n    The result is always a symmetric matrix.\n\n    This calculation uses the out-degree of the graph `G`. For graphs that are not strongly connected, you should\n    first identify their strongly connected components\n    (using :func:`~networkx.algorithms.components.strongly_connected_components`)\n    or attracting components\n    (using :func:`~networkx.algorithms.components.attracting_components`),\n    and then apply this function to those individual components.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    G : NetworkX DiGraph\n        A directed graph\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    bool\n        True if the graph is aperiodic False otherwise\n\n    Raises\n    ------\n    NetworkXError\n        If `G` is not directed\n    NetworkXError\n        If `G` is not strongly connected\n    NetworkXPointlessConcept\n        If `G` has no nodes\n\n    Examples\n    --------\n    A graph consisting of one cycle, the length of which is 2. For example,\n    the following graph contains a cycle ``[4, 2, 3, 1]`` of length 4, which is coprime\n    with the explicitly added cycles of length 3, so the graph is aperiodic::\n\n        >>> DG = nx.DiGraph()\n        >>> nx.add_cycle(DG, [1, 2, 3])\n        >>> nx.add_cycle(DG, [2, 1, 4])\n        >>> nx.is_aperiodic(DG)\n        True\n\n    A single-node graph's aperiodicity depends on whether it has a self-loop:\n    it is aperiodic if a self-loop exists, and periodic otherwise::\n\n        >>> G = nx.DiGraph()\n        >>> G.add_node(1)\n        >>> nx.is_aperiodic(G)\n        False\n        >>> G.add_edge(1, 1)\n        >>> nx.is_aperiodic(G)\n        True\n\n    A Markov chain can be modeled as a directed graph, with nodes representing\n    states and edges representing transitions with non-zero probability.\n    Aperiodicity is typically considered for irreducible Markov chains,\n    which are those that are *strongly connected* as graphs.\n\n    The following Markov chain is irreducible and aperiodic, and thus\n    ergodic. It is guaranteed to have a unique stationary distribution::\n\n        >>> G = nx.DiGraph()\n        >>> nx.add_cycle(G, [1, 2, 3, 4])\n        >>> G.add_edge(1, 3)\n        >>> nx.is_aperiodic(G)\n        True\n\n    Reducible Markov chains can sometimes have a unique stationary distribution.\n    This occurs if the chain has exactly one closed communicating class and\n    that class itself is aperiodic (see [1]_). You can use\n    :func:`~networkx.algorithms.components.attracting_components`\n    to find these closed communicating classes::\n\n        >>> G = nx.DiGraph([(1, 3), (2, 3)])\n        >>> nx.add_cycle(G, [3, 4, 5, 6])\n        >>> nx.add_cycle(G, [3, 5, 6])\n        >>> communicating_classes = list(nx.strongly_connected_components(G))\n        >>> len(communicating_classes)\n        3\n        >>> closed_communicating_classes = list(nx.attracting_components(G))\n        >>> len(closed_communicating_classes)\n        1\n        >>> nx.is_aperiodic(G.subgraph(closed_communicating_classes[0]))\n        True\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    This uses the method outlined in [1]_, which runs in $O(m)$ time\n    given $m$ edges in `G`.\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. [1] Jarvis, J. P.; Shier, D. R. (1996),\n       \"Graph-theoretic analysis of finite Markov chains,\"\n       in Shier, D. R.; Wallenius, K. T., Applied Mathematical Modeling:\n       A Multidisciplinary Approach, CRC Press.\n    \"\"\"\n    if not G.is_directed():\n        raise nx.NetworkXError(\"is_aperiodic not defined for undirected graphs\")\n    if len(G) == 0:\n        raise nx.NetworkXPointlessConcept(\"Graph has no nodes.\")\n    if not nx.is_strongly_connected(G):\n        raise nx.NetworkXError(\"Graph is not strongly connected.\")\n    s = arbitrary_element(G)\n    levels = {s: 0}\n    this_level = [s]\n    g = 0\n    lev = 1\n    while this_level:\n        next_level = []\n        for u in this_level:\n            for v in G[u]:\n                if v in levels:  # Non-Tree Edge\n                    g = gcd(g, levels[u] - levels[v] + 1)\n                else:  # Tree Edge\n                    next_level.append(v)\n                    levels[v] = lev\n        this_level = next_level\n        lev += 1\n    return g == 1\n\n\n@nx._dispatchable(preserve_all_attrs=True, returns_graph=True)\ndef transitive_closure(G, reflexive=False):\n    \"\"\"Returns transitive closure of a graph\n\n    The transitive closure of G = (V,E) is a graph G+ = (V,E+) such that\n    for all v, w in V there is an edge (v, w) in E+ if and only if there\n    is a path from v to w in G.\n\n    Handling of paths from v to v has some flexibility within this definition.\n    A reflexive transitive closure creates a self-loop for the path\n    from v to v of length 0. The result\n        is a reflexive transitive closure of G.\n        If False (the default) non-trivial cycles create self-loops.\n        If None, self-loops are not created.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    NetworkX graph\n        The transitive closure of `G`\n\n    Raises\n    ------\n    NetworkXError\n        If `reflexive` not in `{None, True, False}`\n\n    Examples\n    --------\n    The treatment of trivial (i.e. length 0) cycles is controlled by the\n    `reflexive` parameter.\n\n    Trivial (i.e. length 0) cycles do not create self-loops when\n    ``reflexive=False`` (the default)::\n\n        >>> DG = nx.DiGraph([(1, 2), (2, 3)])\n        >>> TC = nx.transitive_closure(DG, reflexive=False)\n        >>> TC.edges()\n        OutEdgeView([(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)])\n\n    However, nontrivial (i.e. length greater than 0) cycles create self-loops\n    when ``reflexive=False`` (the default)::\n\n        >>> DG = nx.DiGraph([(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1)])\n        >>> TC = nx.transitive_closure(DG, reflexive=False)\n        >>> TC.edges()\n        OutEdgeView([(1, 2), (1, 3), (1, 1), (2, 3), (2, 1), (2, 2), (3, 1), (3, 2), (3, 3)])\n\n    Trivial cycles (length 0) create self-loops when ``reflexive=True``::\n\n        >>> DG = nx.DiGraph([(1, 2), (2, 3)])\n        >>> TC = nx.transitive_closure(DG, reflexive=True)\n        >>> TC.edges()\n        OutEdgeView([(1, 2), (1, 1), (1, 3), (2, 3), (2, 2), (3, 3)])\n\n    And the third option is not to create self-loops at all when ``reflexive=None``::\n\n        >>> DG = nx.DiGraph([(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1)])\n        >>> TC = nx.transitive_closure(DG, reflexive=None)\n        >>> TC.edges()\n        OutEdgeView([(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3), (2, 1), (3, 1), (3, 2)])\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. For this function, each node of in-degree zero in\n    `G` becomes a root of one of the arborescences, and there will be\n    one leaf node for each distinct path from that root to a leaf node\n    in `G`.\n\n    Each node `v` in `G` with *k* parents becomes *k* distinct nodes in\n    the returned branching, one for each parent, and the sub-DAG rooted\n    at `v` is duplicated for each copy. At every\n    step the walk moves from the current node to one of its neighbors\n    (successors for directed graphs) by traversing an edge chosen at random,\n    and the node reached is generated. Without `weight` every edge leaving\n    the current node is equally likely, so parallel edges of a multigraph\n    make a neighbor proportionally more likely and a self-loop is a step that\n    stays at the same node.            return g\n        # try all the versions\n        for version in self.versions:\n            self.set_version(version)\n            g = self.xml.find(f\"{{{self.NS_GEXF}}}graph\")\n def parse_graph(self, graph_xml):\n        \"\"\"Parse a <graph> element into plain records (see `build_graph`).\"\"\"\n        # graph attributes\n        graph_attrs = {}\n        graph_name = As with dicts, the graph should not be updated\nwhile iterating through the view. Views can be iterated multiple times.\n\nEdge and Node views also allow data attribute lookup.\nThe resulting attribute dict is writable as `G.edges[3, 4]['color']='red'`\nDegree views allow lookup of degree values for single nodes.\nWeighted degree is supported with the `weight` argument.\n\nNodeView\n========\n\n    `V = G.nodes` (or `V = G.nodes()`) allows `len(V)`, `n in V`, set\n    operations e.g. \"G.nodes & H.nodes\", and `dd = G.nodes[n]`, where\n    `dd` is the node data dict. Iteration is over the nodes by default.\n\nNodeDataView\n============\n\n    To iterate over (node, data) pairs, use arguments to `G.nodes()`\n    to create a DataView e.g. `DV = G.nodes(data='color', default='red')`.\n    The DataView iterates as `for n, color in DV` and allows\n    `(n, 'red') in DV`. Using `DV = G.nodes(data=True)`, the DataViews\n    use the full datadict in writeable form also allowing contain testing as\n    `(n, {'color': 'red'}) in VD`. DataViews allow set operations when\n    data attributes are hashable.\n\nDegreeView\n==========\n\n    `V = G.degree` allows iteration over (node, degree) pairs as well\n    as lookup: `deg=V[n]`. There are many flavors of DegreeView\n    for In/Out/Directed/Multi. For Directed Graphs, `G.degree`\n    counts both in and out going edges. `G.out_degree` and\n    `G.in_degree` count only specific directions.\n    Weighted degree using edge data attributes is provide via\n    `V = G.degree(weight='attr_name')` where any string with the\n    attribute name can be used. `weight=None` is the default.\n    No set operations are implemented for degrees, use NodeView.\n\n    The argument `nbunch` restricts iteration to nodes in nbunch.\n    The DegreeView can still lookup any node even if nbunch is specified.\n\nEdgeView\n========\n\n    `V = G.edges` or `V = G.edges()` allows iteration over edges as well as\n    `e in V`, set operations and edge data lookup `dd = G.edges[2, 3]`.\n    Iteration is over 2-tuples `(u, v)` for Graph/DiGraph. For multigraphs\n    edges 3-tuples `(u, v, key)` are the default but 2-tuples can be obtained\n    via `V = G.edges(keys=False)`.\n\n    Set operations for directed graphs treat the edges as a set of 2-tuples.\n    For undirected graphs, 2-tuples are not a unique representation of edges.\n    So long as the set being compared to contains unique representations\n    of its edges, the set operations will act as expected. If the other\n    set contains both `(0, 1)` and `(1, 0)` however, the result of set\n    operations may contain both representations of the same edge.\n\nEdgeDataView\n============\n\n    Edge data can be reported using an EdgeDataView typically created\n    by calling an EdgeView: `DV = G.edges(data='weight', default=1)`.\n    The EdgeDataView allows iteration over edge tuples, membership checking\n    but no set operations.\n\n    Iteration depends on `data` and `default` and for multigraph `keys`\n    If `data is False` (the default) then iterate over 2-tuples `(u, v)`.\n    If `data is True` iterate over 3-tuples `(u, v, datadict)`.\n    Otherwise iterate over `(u, v, datadict.get(data, default))`.\n    For Multigraphs, if `keys is True`, replace `u, v` with `u, v, key`\n    to create 3-tuples and 4-tuples.\n\n    The argument `nbunch` restricts edges to those incident to nodes in nbunch.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport weakref\nfrom abc import ABC\nfrom collections.abc import Mapping, Set\n\nimport networkx as nx\n\n__all__ = [\n    \"NodeView\",\n    \"NodeDataView\",\n    \"EdgeView\",\n    \"OutEdgeView\",\n    \"InEdgeView\",\n    \"EdgeDataView\",\n    \"OutEdgeDataView\",\n    \"InEdgeDataView\",\n    \"MultiEdgeView\",\n    \"OutMultiEdgeView\",\n    \"InMultiEdgeView\",\n    \"MultiEdgeDataView\",\n    \"OutMultiEdgeDataView\",\n    \"InMultiEdgeDataView\",\n    \"DegreeView\",\n    \"DiDegreeView\",\n    \"InDegreeView\",\n    \"OutDegreeView\",\n    \"MultiDegreeView\",\n    \"DiMultiDegreeView\",\n    \"InMultiDegreeView\",\n    \"OutMultiDegreeView\",\n]\n\n\ndef _nbunch_iter(nodes, nbunch=None):\n    \"\"\"Returns an iterator over the nodes in `nbunch` that are also in `nodes`.\n\n    This is the node-bunch iteration behind :meth:`Graph.nbunch_iter\n    <networkx.Graph.nbunch_iter>`.
